entries.test: Public demonstrations of AI capabilities in 2025 and GPT-5 hallucination evaluations would test the factual assertions.
entries.note: “Underwhelming” is evaluative; the AGI and hallucination assertions are factual.

entries.test: Contemporary LLM reliability evaluations and public revenue, cost, and profitability reports would test the stated reliability and economic concerns.
entries.note: “Look dubious” is a qualitative assessment, but the claim has an empirical core.

entries.test: AI companies' financial reports and evidence of durable technical advantages over competitors as of December 2025 would test both assertions.
entries.note: The Nvidia exception applies to profitability, not to the technical-moat assertion.

entries.test: Changes in OpenAI's advantage over competitors on public capability evaluations and product adoption through December 2025 would test whether its lead substantially narrowed.
Public scaling results and contemporaneous statements or surveys of AI researchers would test diminishing returns and declining confidence in scaling to AGI.
entries.note: The normalization removes “Many would agree,” presenting the first clause more categorically.

entries.test: Trends in neurosymbolic research publications, funding, and prominent deployments through December 2025 would show whether its prominence was increasing.
Public demonstrations scored against the Marcus-Brundage task requirements would establish whether any system solved more than four by the post's publication.
entries.note: The four-task ceiling is firm; the suggestion that none were solved is explicitly uncertain.

entries.test: Independent 2025 agent evaluations and documented deployment failure rates would test whether agents reliably completed their intended tasks.
Marcus's published list of seventeen high-confidence 2025 predictions and his public retrospective scoring would establish whether he counted sixteen as correct.
entries.note: This preserves his self-scoring qualification; it does not establish independent agreement with that score.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and independent evaluations would establish whether broadly general human-level AI was achieved during 2026 or 2027.
entries.note: The full forecast runs through the end of 2027.
The central claim of a markedly shifted “vibe” lacks a shared test. The named individuals' statements are separately verifiable.

entries.test: Public records of 2026 consumer availability, deliveries, and independently documented home use of humanoid robots would distinguish substantial products from predominantly demonstrations.
Published 2026 robot demonstrations and independent home trials documenting task completion, failures, and human intervention would test the forecast.
entries.note: Marcus asserts this himself while citing Brooks in support.

entries.test: Comparative public evaluations of leading generative AI systems and their deployment through 2026 would show whether one country established a clear, sustained advantage.
Changes from 2025 to 2026 in research publications, funding, staffing, and projects involving world models and neurosymbolic AI would test increased activity.
Subsequent valuation histories and financial retrospectives would establish whether 2025 became recognized as the bubble peak and the start of Wall Street's loss of confidence.
entries.note: No deadline is specified for the retrospective judgment.

entries.test: Subsequent AI valuation declines and financial retrospectives identifying the September 2025 Oracle surge and its aftermath as the downturn's beginning would test the forecast.
entries.note: The normalization omits “and what has happened since” from the predicted turning point. Further rises are optional; the eventual decline is asserted.

entries.test: Changes from 2025 to 2026 in polling, protests, organized opposition, and political campaigns against generative AI and AI deregulation would test whether backlash escalated.
Campaign platforms, advertising, debates, and election coverage from the 2026 US midterms and earlier elections would establish whether AI became an election issue for the first time.
entries.note: The “first time” assertion also requires comparison with earlier elections.
“May eventually” expresses a possibility, not a firm forecast.

entries.test: Public outcomes and consistent scoring of Marcus's 2025 and 2026 prediction lists would establish whether the latter achieved a lower accuracy rate.
entries.note: “I don't expect” states a firm expectation here. The accompanying explanation about intellectual climate is more subjective.
There is no shared test for the field's overall intellectual climate becoming more fluid, realistic, and open-minded.
The normalization adds an explicit comparative likelihood claim. Neither the intellectual climate nor “genuine progress” has a shared test in this formulation.
